newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Irish inflation seen up slightly in March.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Irish inflation seen up slightly in March.

text.p: Irish consumer prices should tick up slightly in March as the winter sales effect unwinds but CPI data, due for release at 1100 GMT (1200 local time) on Thursday, should confirm that Ireland's inflation outlook remains benign, analysts said on Monday.
Most analysts expect a monthly rise of 0.3 percent after a 0.6 percent increase in February for a year-on-year rise of 1.5 percent.

Forecasting an annual rate for March is more complicated as Ireland's CSO only began publishing monthly consumer price data this year and a comparable monthly estimate for March 1996 is not available.
The figures therefore have to be compared with the reading for the first quarter of last year, taken in the middle of February.

"The move to monthly data this year means that a 12-month year-on-year rate cannot be calculated so the best that we can do is offer a 13-month rate which we see at 1.9 percent," Riada Stockbrokers said. "This, of course, overstates the true '12-month year-on-year' rate."
Other forecasts are in a range of 1.8 to 1.9 percent.
Analysts say the primary focus will be on whether or not there has been any impact on prices as a result of the seven percent fall in the Irish pound against sterling since last August.
"Our own limited supermarket survey would lead us to believe that there has been no impact yet on food prices," the bond unit at AIB Group Treasury said in a research note.
"Indeed we found, if anything, that there has been a slight fall in food prices since February."
Analysts will also be keen to see if there has been an unusually sharp rebound in clothing and footwear prices after a 5.6 percent drop year-on-year in February.

"A very sharp pick-up in prices in this sector in March would be of concern as it would suggest that the low February figure was due just to a prolonged sales effect or a short-term phenomenon reflecting the opening of new (UK) retail outlets," AIB said.
Although the data are expected to confirm that Irish inflationary pressures remain subdued, they should not lead to any change in Irish interest rate policy in the short-term, analysts say.

The Central Bank will want to see the CPI data for the first half of 1997 before it is fully convinced that a low inflation rate is in prospect this year, particularly as Irish credit growth remains strong.
Analysts say the May figures are critical in this regard as they are the next set of data which will provide an exact year-on-year comparison.
